fields.title: Polka: permissions requested by retail chains
fields.summary: Three chains ask for roles: staff see their own data, management sees everything. Currently, there is only one role.
fields.decisionPrompt: What do we do? State the price of your decision.
fields.brief/role: You are a product manager at Polka.
fields.brief/company: Polka is a fictional grocery delivery service from local stores: 900 partner stores, a buyer app, and a partner dashboard.
fields.brief/context: You are a product manager at Polka. Three chains independently asked for the same thing: staff should only see their own store, while management sees everything. Currently, the permissions model is simple: a store administrator sees everything for that store, with no other roles. For a chain with 40 stores, this means 40 disconnected accounts.
fields.brief/objective: Provide chains with an access model that addresses both their requests and their security questionnaires.
fields.brief/constraints: A chain manager currently logs in using forty accounts. Flexible rules take eight weeks.
fields.brief/task: Decide what you are doing and state what remains on the client's side.
fields.learnTakeaway/title: Access models are designed around roles, not flexibility
fields.learnTakeaway/body: Requests for "flexible permissions" almost always boil down to three or four roles and a single scope axis. Flexibility costs twice as much and introduces a configuration UI that must be maintained and explained. Look at corporate questionnaires: they usually contain the second half of the requirements—audit logs and access revocation—and part of that fundamentally lives on the client side.
fields.evidenceCards/0/content: Cashier—shift orders. Store manager—their store. Chain manager—everything. Accountant—financial data, without buyer details.
fields.evidenceCards/1/content: Only one role. A chain manager logs in under 40 accounts.
fields.evidenceCards/2/content: "Roles plus scope—3 weeks. Flexible rules—8 weeks. Single sign-on via client directory—6 weeks."
fields.evidenceCards/3/content: All three corporate questionnaires include items on roles, access revocation upon dismissal, and audit logs.
fields.decisionOptions/0/description: Three weeks. Four roles, scope is either store or chain.
fields.decisionOptions/0/consequence: covers all three requests. Does not solve revocation upon dismissal—that remains a manual action for the client administrator. Does not provide an audit log.
fields.decisionOptions/1/label: Roles plus scope, plus audit log, plus inactive user reminders
fields.decisionOptions/1/description: Roles plus scope, plus audit log, plus inactive user reminders. Five weeks.
fields.decisionOptions/1/consequence: covers requests and two questionnaire items. Revocation remains with the client, but includes a reminder mechanism.
fields.decisionOptions/2/consequence: covers any future requests. Requires a configuration UI that is a product in its own right. None of the three chains requested this level of complexity.
fields.decisionOptions/3/description: Single sign-on via client directory. Six weeks.
fields.decisionOptions/3/consequence: radically solves revocation upon dismissal—access terminates along with the corporate account. Does not solve roles: they are still needed.
fields.rubric/remediation/0/gap: Does not apply the principle of least privilege
fields.rubric/remediation/1/gap: Does not distinguish between authentication and access revocation
fields.rubric/remediation/2/gap: Does not account for data sensitivity in the dashboard
fields.rubric/remediation/3/gap: Secrets and access controls are not treated as part of the product permissions model
